2210.01892|superposition.author: Kshitij Sachan
2210.01892|superposition.quote: The relationship between increasing/decreasing marginal returns and polysemanticity generalizes beyond our toy model. However, we don't have a generic technique to define capacity across different architectures and loss functions.

2210.01892|superposition.author: Adam Jermyn
2210.01892|superposition.quote: As long as you know what the features are you can calculate dL/dC_i for each feature and figure out what's going on with that. The main challenge to this is feature identification: in a one layer model with synthetic data it's often easy to know what the features are. In more complicated settings it's much less clear what the "right" or "natural" features are...

2211.09169|superposition.author: Adam Jermyn
2211.09169|superposition.quote: I think my expectation is that the number of features exceeds the number of neurons in real-world settings, but that it might be possible to arrange for the number of neurons to exceed the number of important features ... We haven't really pinned this down, and it may also depend on the initialization/training procedure (as we saw when k > N), so it's definitely worth a thorough look.

2309.08600|superposition.author: Hoagy
2309.08600|superposition.quote: we did not find a working CUDA-compatible version and used the scikit version you mention. This meant that the data volumes used are somewhat limited - still on the order of a million examples but 10-50x less than went into the autoencoders.
2309.08600|superposition.summary: The ICA baseline, which cannot be overcomplete, got 10–50x less data than the SAEs.

2312.03096|superposition.author: Rohin Shah
2312.03096|superposition.quote: In particular, I think it is likely very sensitive to the implicit assumption that feature i and feature j never co-occur on a single input. ... My prediction would be that polysemanticity goes down very significantly (probably to zero if the probabilities are high enough and the training is done for long enough).
2312.03096|superposition.summary: An author replies that unrelated features rarely co-occur.

2408.05451|superposition.author: Lucius Bushnaq
2408.05451|superposition.quote: If basically all we can do with the 'superposed variables' is make lookup tables of them, there didn't seem to me to be much need for the concept at all to reverse engineer neural networks. Just stick with the summary variables, summarising is what intelligence is all about. If we can do actual, general computation with the sparse variables? ... Well, that would change things.
2408.05451|superposition.summary: A self-described superposition skeptic, conditional on the paper's error analysis holding up.

2408.05451|superposition.author: LawrenceC
2408.05451|superposition.quote: My guess is that most computations are indeed closer to continuous than to boolean. While it's possible to construct boolean interpretations of bigram circuits or induction heads, my impression (having not looked at either in detail on real models) is that neither of these cleanly occur inside LMs.

2408.05451|superposition.author: jake_mendel
2408.05451|superposition.quote: We certainly don't expect that real neural networks implement our constructions with weights that are exactly 0 or 1. Rather, neural networks probably do a messier thing which is (potentially substantially) more efficient, and we are not making predictions about the quantitative sizes of errors at a fixed d.

2408.05451|superposition.author: Lucius Bushnaq
2408.05451|superposition.quote: But as currently written, it doesn't seem like I can use the outputs of one layer performing a subset of ANDs as the inputs of another layer performing another subset of ANDs. ... Talked it through with Jake. Bias setoff can help, but it currently looks to us like you still end up with AND gates that share a variable systematically having positive sign in their inner product.
2408.05451|superposition.summary: So layers of these constructions are not yet shown to stack.

2409.14507|superposition.author: Joseph Bloom
2409.14507|superposition.quote: I see it as doubling down on sparsity and a single decomposition, both of which I think may just not reflect the underlying data generating process.
2409.14507|superposition.summary: Elsewhere in the thread they frame the work more narrowly, as SAE measurement error.

2502.16681|superposition.author: Lewis Smith et al. (GDM mech interp team)
2502.16681|superposition.quote: Dense linear probes perform nearly perfectly, including out of distribution. ... Linear probes trained only on the SAE reconstruction are also significantly worse than linear probes on the residual stream OOD, suggesting that SAEs are discarding information relevant to the target concept
2502.16681|superposition.summary: A parallel GDM study on Gemma-2-9B, with some authors shared.

web:already-clean|superposition.author: Adam Scherlis
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: But in fact, cosine similarities between feature vectors have rich semantic content ... Features aren't just crammed together arbitrarily; they're grouped with similar features.

web:already-clean|superposition.author: Neel Nanda
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: For neuron/computational superposition, it seems to me like language models have far more facts and memorized things in them than they have neurons. ... I expect that weak neuron activations contain lots of semantic superposition-y info, which, if ablated, would meaningfully damage network performance.

web:already-clean|superposition.author: Manic Pixie
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: Showing that most neurons in a model encode one primary concept is not the same as showing that most concepts a model knows are represented by one neuron. Qwen3-32B has only tens of thousands of neurons per layer, right?

web:already-clean|superposition.author: Shiva's Right Foot
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: In my exploration of gpt2 -xl, I haven't really encountered neurons that are polysemantic in that way. Many times neurons signify a somewhat abstract concept which has many different instantiations in text

web:already-clean|superposition.author: leogao
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: My best guess from all the results I've seen is that ablating small neuron activations quite substantially degrades model performance, so I don’t think we get to ignore weak activations completely. ... If you can’t simulate the neuron in a way that doesn’t degrade the model, you don’t really understand the neuron.
web:already-clean|superposition.summary: They ask for KL-based simulation scores before the ~90% figure is trusted.

web:already-clean|superposition.author: Julian Bradshaw
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: What we see in the Colorado neuron is instead decreasing activations for increasingly less-related concepts, exactly the branching pattern Nick's idea predicts. (~87% of activations >50% of max are directly Colorado-related.)
web:already-clean|superposition.summary: Checked in the essay's released data; this answers the Tornado counterexample.

web:already-clean|superposition.author: StefanHex
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: I find the evidence against superposition less convincing because many experiments are doing extreme compressions (retraining a layer down to 10 neurons), and take the absence of superposition as evidence against superposition in realistic settings. However, it is quite established that superposition (and computation in superposition) only really works in high dimensions / for large numbers of neurons, so I wouldn't have expected superposition in their the very-low dimension experiment.

web:already-clean|superposition.author: Brangus
web:already-clean|superposition.quote: I had Claude check what else it tracks: Tornado’s Python HTTP client code, just as hard. ... If you force Qwen to pick a US state that it most associates with Tornado, it assigns 59% to Colorado. If you zero out this neuron, that drops to 15%.
web:already-clean|superposition.summary: Others in the thread dispute 'just as hard'.

web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.author: nostalgebraist
web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.quote: In the paper, the MLP that is decomposed into features is the last sub-block in the network. ... Yet, the second view -- in which features are fundamentally directions in logit-update space -- seems closer to the way the autoencoder works mechanistically.
web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.summary: The decomposed MLP feeds the logits directly, so many 'features' may be logit-update directions rather than inputs packed into 512 neurons; they note deeper-layer results suggest it isn't only this.

web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.author: Neel Nanda
web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.quote: The core results seem to replicate - I trained a sparse autoencoder on the MLP layer of an open source 1 layer GELU language model, and a significant fraction of the latent space features were interpretable
web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.summary: 60% of the replicated latents fall in an uninterpretable ultra-low-frequency cluster.

web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.author: Neel Nanda
web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.quote: However, a significant majority of features seem to be fairly dense in the neuron basis! ... But this seems like evidence that being dense in the neuron basis is the norm, not the exception.
web:towards-monosemanticity|superpositio.summary: About 92% of features; kurtosis still shows a privileged neuron basis, and they cannot rule out SAE noise.

web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.author: Eric J. Michaud
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.quote: We also looked at ~2000 Mistral-7B clusters and only the days of the week and months of the year clusters seemed clearly interesting. So at least for the LLMs we looked at, for the SAEs we had, and with our method for discovering interesting geometry, interesting geometry didn't seem ubiquitous.
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.summary: An Engels et al. author. The same comment agrees that the near-orthogonal picture from Toy Models is wrong.

web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.author: Adam Scherlis
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.quote: it says that the total amount of correlation between a given feature and all other features (i.e. interference from them) matters, but which other features are interfering with it doesn't matter, and the particular amount of interference from each other feature doesn't matter either. This version of the hypothesis seems pretty well falsified at this point.

web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.author: Adam Scherlis
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.quote: the full set of correlations is nearly equivalent to the embeddings themselves, and has all of the interesting parts. ... I don't think I've heard of an improved theory yet.
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.summary: A review 18 months on that otherwise says the post holds up.

web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.author: Eric Winsor
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.quote: GPT-2-small uses a cosine/sine spiral for its learned positional embeddings embeddings, and I don't think I've seen a mechanistic/dynamical explanation for this

web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.author: Jake Mendel
web:sae-feature-geometry|superposition.quote: I think the embedding at layer 0 is a good place for thinking about the kind of structure that the superposition hypothesis is blind to. ... But those embeddings aren't random! They have been carefully learned and contain lots of useful information.

2305.04388|cot.author: Miles Turpin
2305.04388|cot.quote: A qualitative finding that we didn't put in the paper was that key discrepancies in the explanations that lead models to support the biased answer instead of the correct answer in many cases come near the end of the explanation. Sometimes the model does normal reasoning, and then gives some caveat or makes a mistake at the end, that leads it to ultimately give the biased prediction.

2305.04388|cot.author: nostalgebraist
2305.04388|cot.quote: If we don't specify what we want, we get the human default ... and the human default is "unfaithful" in the sense of Turpin et al. ... But we... can just specify what we want? Or try to?
2305.04388|cot.summary: Written after he retracted his post's summary of Turpin et al. (that the CoT stays roughly constant).

2307.13702|cot.author: Sam Bowman
2307.13702|cot.quote: I don't think our results clearly show that faithfulness goes down with model size, just that there's less affirmative evidence for faithfulness at larger model sizes, at least in part for predictable reasons related to the metric design.

2307.13702|cot.author: nostalgebraist
2307.13702|cot.quote: In constructed cases like these, one has to lie in order to exhibit this property. One has to say the answer one knows is false, as though that answer were true.
2307.13702|cot.summary: On the adding-mistakes test, for questions easy enough to need no CoT.

2404.15758|cot.author: Brendan Long
2404.15758|cot.quote: I now think this paper should be taken as evidence against LLMs ability to perform long-term reasoning ... in secret ... However, if the problem requires step-by-step thinking and the model isn't deep enough, filler tokens don't help.

2404.15758|cot.author: ryan_greenblatt
2404.15758|cot.quote: Filler tokens don't allow for serially deeper cognition than what architectural limits allow (n-layers of processing), but they could totally allow for solving a higher fraction of "heavily serial" reasoning tasks

2505.05410|cot.author: ryan_greenblatt
2505.05410|cot.quote: This paper exposes unfaithfulness in cases where the non-visible reasoning is extremely minimal such that it can easily happen within a forward pass (e.g. a simple reward hack or an easy-to-notice hint). However, a lot of my hope for CoT faithfulness comes from cases where the reasoning is sufficiently difficult and serially deep that the model would have to reason in CoT for the reasoning to occur.

2505.05410|cot.author: GradientDissenter
2505.05410|cot.quote: We can almost always detect whether a clue was used to solve the question by looking at the CoT, even when the CoT is unfaithful.
2505.05410|cot.summary: METR replicated the Claude 3.7 Sonnet result within error, then added harder free-response clues; a CoT-reading detector caught clue use at 99.3% TPR (96.2% specificity). To get enough clue use they relied on what they call a rather unnatural prompt.

2503.11926|cot.author: Thomas Kwa
2503.11926|cot.quote: It is unclear how this applies to cheating / other malicious behaviors that are hard enough that they require CoT.

2503.11926|cot.author: Caleb Biddulph
2503.11926|cot.quote: The model apparently decides to skip the test only at the very end of its CoT, slipping its decision in very briefly: ... This is sort of like steganography, but not the completely hidden, multi-step steganographic reasoning I was thinking of.

2505.23575|cot.author: Rohin Shah
2505.23575|cot.quote: My sense is that there's some baseline level of capability that is required to be a good monitor ... which includes the capacity to consider the hypothesis that the information you've been given is false, and that non-frontier LLMs often don't meet it.

2505.23575|cot.author: Nicholas Goldowsky-Dill
2505.23575|cot.quote: I worry that several of the "subtle" tasks might not be that hard for an action-only monitor to catch given proper prompting, but aren't clearly within scope for the current monitor.
2505.23575|cot.summary: His examples are the "Long implementation" and "Variable name" side tasks.

2505.23575|cot.author: Nathan Helm-Burger
2505.23575|cot.quote: For example, the fine-tuned malicious model had a 0% chance of getting caught on subtle tasks by the monitor not using CoT. With CoT, that went up to like 3% catch rate.

2507.05246|cot.author: Jozdien
2507.05246|cot.quote: My guess is that how faithful a model's CoT is in some setting is highly dependent on propensity—in a setting where a model has a strong desire to not state something explicitly in its CoT, I'd expect models to perform much better at passing information implicitly.
2507.05246|cot.summary: He cites alignment faking, where the CoT actively misled about behaviour.

2507.05246|cot.author: Rohin Shah
2507.05246|cot.quote: Okay, that position seems to me equivalent to the position that models will be more capable at evading monitors when they intrinsically want to evade monitors, than when they are explicitly prompted to evade monitors. ... That position seems pretty unlikely to me (for current models). Models are trained really hard to follow instructions in the prompt to the best of their ability.

2507.05246|cot.author: arav-dhoot
2507.05246|cot.quote: Across 11 models from 6 families (not just Gemini), models follow simple hints unfaithfully well above baseline, but complex hints that require computation are followed near baseline.
2507.05246|cot.summary: The post also finds CoT-necessity is per model, not per task: multi-digit multiplication needs no CoT for Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.5, so the paper's complex hints may not force CoT in stronger models.

2507.05246|cot.author: Vincent Cheng
2507.05246|cot.quote: Similar to the original paper, we see that models are unable to evade even monitors weaker than themselves without heavily losing accuracy.
2507.05246|cot.summary: METR replication with Claude and GPT actors.

2507.05246|cot.author: Vincent Cheng
2507.05246|cot.quote: This GDM paper uses chain-of-thought to mean the response from a reasoning model with reasoning mode turned off and being prompted with "Think step-by-step."

2507.11473|cot.author: ryan_greenblatt
2507.11473|cot.quote: Do reasoning models default to having good grammar in their thoughts? (Even when they are trained to have shorter reasoning.)
2507.11473|cot.summary: His example is a terse, ungrammatical OpenAI trace, which challenges the position paper's premise that a natural-language prior keeps CoT legible.

2507.11473|cot.author: Brendan Long
2507.11473|cot.quote: I think there's a lot of evidence that CoT from reasoning models is also subject to the same selection pressures, it also limits the trustworthiness, and this isn't a small effect.
2507.11473|cot.summary: His evidence is that Claude can be asked to reason in Spanish or toward a wrong answer, so reasoning CoT faces the same helpful/harmless pressure as outputs.

2511.11584|cot.author: ryan_greenblatt
2511.11584|cot.quote: The results here don't correspond to the AI learning to reason steganographically.

2511.11584|cot.author: Rohin Shah
2511.11584|cot.quote: The reward hack is easy to execute (likely doesn't require reasoning, or only very little reasoning) ... The reward function is deliberately designed to cause obfuscation, and is about as close to process-based as you can get while not looking directly at the thoughts.

2511.11584|cot.author: lukemarks
2511.11584|cot.quote: On the point regarding unconditionally down-weighting the penalized word, this was our primary motivation for trying the judge penalty. We agree that it is a strong reason to be skeptical of the regex penalty results in isolation.
2511.11584|cot.summary: Replying to Tomek Korbak: a one-word regex penalty may just lower that token's probability everywhere.

2511.11584|cot.author: jacob_drori
2511.11584|cot.quote: Therefore we interpret the polynomial environment as an example where training against an output monitor caused a big change to the sort of reasoning being done in the CoT. As you note, it is not an example of obfuscation.

web:openai-monitorability-evals|cot.author: Connor Dilgren
web:openai-monitorability-evals|cot.quote: For each model and dataset combination, most instances never survive filtering in any of the 100 draws. The low eligibility makes it difficult to trust the downstream monitorability estimation, especially given the already-small sizes of the datasets before filtering.
web:openai-monitorability-evals|cot.summary: On MATH only 3-5% of instances were eligible for DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, and each model is scored on a different subset, so cross-model comparisons are hard.

web:openai-monitorability-evals|cot.author: Connor Dilgren
web:openai-monitorability-evals|cot.quote: we find that models are, surprisingly, often capable of producing valid solutions that meet the "impossible" requirement. ... Both solution length evaluations see an increase in g-mean ... by about 17 percentage points moving from the most inclusive to the least inclusive "actual hack" set.
web:openai-monitorability-evals|cot.summary: Re-running the impossible-coding evals with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, they find label noise that biases measured monitorability downward.
